            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(8)</span></span><span>The bioeconomy is able to provide sustainable biomass and bio-based solutions for industrial production. The Commission communication “A Strategic Framework for a Competitive and Sustainable EU Bioeconomy”</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref26" href="#footnote26">26</a>
               </span><span> identifies lead markets, such as bio-based plastics and polymers, bio-based chemicals and biobased construction products, as well as lead technologies</span><span> </span><span>that can support </span><span>the Union’s</span><span> </span><span>strategic autonomy and the decarbonisation of the industrial sectors identified in this initiative.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(9)</span></span><span>The automotive industry is a cornerstone of the Union economy</span><span>. </span><span>With a view to </span><span>delivering</span><span> on the Union’s climate policy objectives, over the past years, the European automotive industry has been investing heavily in the development of cleaner vehicles and innovative components. </span><span>Electric vehicles and electric vehicle components, including traction batteries, e-powertrain components and electronic systems, are essential technologies for advancing the decarbonisation of road transport.</span><span> However, as a result of costs disadvantage and the transformation of the value chain with an increasing value share for batteries, e-powertrain and electronics, the level of Union content in vehicles produced in the Union is decreasing. </span><span>It</span><span> is no longer possible to postpone e</span><span>ffective measures </span><span>to avoid the risk of </span><span>local production being displaced.</span><span> </span><span>In the absence of such measures, the current circumstances would lead to a full reliance on third countries for key vehicle components. </span><span>That would be</span><span> a serious threat to the Union’s economic security and future resilience, as well as for its climate goals. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(10)</span></span><span>The unpredictability, complexity and, at times, excessive length of national permit-granting procedures undermine the </span><span>cost</span><span>-effectiveness of</span><span> investments necessary for the development of industrial activities. </span><span>T</span><span>herefore</span><span>, and</span><span> in order to ensure and speed up </span><span>the</span><span> effective implementation </span><span>of</span><span> industrial manufacturing activities</span><span>,</span><span> </span><span>Member States should apply streamlined and digitalised permit-granting processes. A competent authority should coordinate all permit granting processes and issue a comprehensive decision within the applicable time limit.</span><span> </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(11)</span></span><span>The implementation of single </span><span>access points</span><span> should be based on the European Business Wallets established pursuant to [Proposal </span><span>for a</span><span> Regulation on the establishment of European Business Wallets</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref27" href="#footnote27">27</a>
               </span><span>], as they provide a secure, standardised, and interoperable platform for businesses to interact with public sector bodies. This should enable the efficient and effective submission of applications, while ensuring a high level of data protection, cybersecurity, and integrity of information. The European Business Wallets will also enable the streamlining of investments that were made and the avoidance of unnecessary duplications, allowing for the optimisation of resources and the reduction of administrative burdens for businesses.</span><span> </span><span>The implementation of single access points should also, to the extent possible, use existing Union digital infrastructures, catalogues and building blocks, including those developed under the Once-Only Technical System and its implementing acts. This would promote complementarity, interoperability and the efficient use of public resources, while avoiding duplication of existing digital solutions.</span><span> </span>
            </p>
         </div>
         <div class="content">
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(12)</span></span><span>In </span><span>order to ensure streamlined and simplified permit-granting procedures, a </span><span>single</span><span> application covering all necessary permits </span><span>should be</span><span> </span><span>provided</span><span> for all industrial manufacturing projects</span><span> except for the manufacturing sector under the C12 code.</span><span> </span><span>It</span><span> should </span><span>not </span><span>apply w</span><span>here specific permit-granting or licensing procedures or requirements are established in Union harmonisation legislation for industrial manufacturing projects, such as pursuant to Regulation</span><span>s</span><span> (EU) 2024/1735</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref28" href="#footnote28">28</a>
               </span><span> and </span><span>(</span><span>EU</span><span>)</span><span> 2024/1252</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref29" href="#footnote29">29</a>
               </span><span> </span><span>of the European Parliament and of the Council</span><span>.</span><span> </span><span>Sectorial </span><span>Union</span><span> legislation governing medicines and medical devices has recently undergone or is undergoing further streamlining of harmonised rules and timelines for authorisations and certifications, with options to speed up the process if necessary. Those rules should therefore not be considered permit-granting procedures within the context of this initiative.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(13)</span></span><span>Regulation (EU) [202X/XX]</span><span> </span><span>of […]</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref30" href="#footnote30">30</a>
               </span><span> </span><span>establishes a common acceleration framework for environmental assessments in order to boost the Union’s roll out of key technologies, reduce dependencies and strengthen competitiveness. Procedures linked to environmental assessments should be accelerated and streamlined for plans, programmes and projects across all sectors of the economy while maintaining high levels of protection of human health and of the environment. Some sectors may, however, require yet faster environmental assessments. Therefore, and in order to safeguard the coherence of the legal framework of environmental assessments, while allowing for the additional needs for acceleration in certain strategic sectors, Regulation (EU) [202X/XX] establishes a dedicated toolbox that should therefore be used in the context of this Regulation. </span><span>Given their essential role in ensuring the achievement of the Union’s climate objectives, and their contribution to the Union’s resilience and economic security, energy-intensive industry decarbonisation projects, industrial manufacturing projects located in industrial manufacturing acceleration areas, and net-zero technology projects should be considered strategic projects within the meaning of Regulation (EU) [202X/XX</span><span>] </span><span>and therefore benefit from the dedicated toolbox established under that Regulation.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(14)</span></span><span>Regulation (EU) 2024/1735</span><span> </span><span>sets out provisions that streamline administrative and permit-granting processes for net-zero technology manufacturing projects. Some specific components in the supply chain of net-zero technologies are produced through energy</span><span>-</span><span>intensive production processes. Energy</span><span>-</span><span>intensive industry decarbonisation projects fall within the scope of Regulation (EU) 2024/1735 where the relevant facilities produce components that are part of the supply chain of a net-zero technology. However, energy</span><span>-</span><span>intensive facilities that do not produce components that are used in net-zero technologies are currently excluded from the scope of Regulation (EU) 2024/1735. Th</span><span>is</span><span> creates the risk of </span><span>uneven conditions of </span><span>between energy</span><span>-</span><span>intensive industries and slows down decarbonisation efforts</span><span>.</span><span> All energy-intensive decarbonisation projects should therefore be subject to the same permit-granting processes. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(15)</span></span><span>T</span><span>he Union should adopt a more strategic approach in leveraging its economic weight and the value of access to its internal market. In </span><span>that</span><span> context, </span><span>t</span><span>he strategic use of public intervention is </span><span>essential to prevent critical dependencies in the Union</span><span>. Public procurement amounts to 15% of the Union’s GDP. Contracting authorities and entities should therefore, where appropriate, ensure that public procurement requirements foster economic security and resilience of supply chains. Public support schemes also play an important role in stimulating demand in downstream sectors that account for a significant share of demand for certain strategic products and technologies. </span><span>Such</span><span> schemes should therefore favour beneficiaries that make a greater contribution to strengthening the Union’s resilience and advancing its decarbonisation objectives. Auctions are </span><span>crucial</span><span> for the deployment of net-zero technologies and should be designed to foster demand for such technologies including components originating from the Union.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(16)</span></span><span>The </span><span>Union and Member States maintain an open investment environment, as enshrined in the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union </span><span>(TFEU)</span><span> and embedded in their international commitments. </span><span>This includes commitments u</span><span>nder the</span><span> </span><span>World Trade Organisation</span><span> Agreement on</span><span> Government Procurement (GPA)</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref31" href="#footnote31">31</a>
               </span><span>, as well as bilateral trade agreements, </span><span>to open public procurement procedures and other forms of public intervention. At the same time, </span><span>the Union retains the right to apply general or security exceptions. </span><span>The Commission will regularly assess whether the conditions for excluding a third country from the scope of the provisions deeming content originating in third countries to be equivalent to Union origin, are in place, and will take appropriate action. </span><span>Economic security aims at protecting and strengthening the internal market. Member States cannot rely on economic security to prevent, condition, or otherwise hinder in any way investments coming from other Member States</span><span>. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(17)</span></span><span>The </span><span>progressive integration of candidate countries and potential candidates into the Union’s internal market, including through their gradual participation in Union policies and programmes, is essential to support their alignment with the acquis, strengthen their competitiveness, promote their deeper integration into Union value chains and enhance the Union’s economic security. This Regulation should therefore contribute to fostering such gradual integration, including by facilitating the participation of economic operators from those countries in Union-wide value chains, Union public procurement, public support schemes and auctions where appropriate and in line with the Union’s interests and objectives. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(18)</span></span><span>Acknowledging the importance of the Union’s advancing towards greater strategic autonomy and resilience, the Union should also </span><span>recognise for reasons of coherence the proactive efforts of partner countries to prioritise domestic</span><span> participation in economic activities, similar to the measures established within this </span><span>Regulation. In the context of implementing </span><span>Union origin</span><span> requirements within certain categories of public procurement and public schemes procedures, the Union should thoughtfully consider partner countries’ content conditions</span><span> for strategic Union-funded or supported investments in these partner countries, accepting its presence. This strategic approach is expected to enhance mutual economic benefits, strengthen strategic partnerships, and align with the Union’s overarching objectives of international partnerships.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(19)</span></span><span>Demand-side measures </span><span>should focus on establishing low-carbon requirements</span><span> </span><span>for steel, cement </span><span>and</span><span> aluminium used in buildings, infrastructure and</span><span> motor vehicles</span><span>, where appropriate</span><span>, since those sectors are the most energy-intensive </span><span>industries. Targeted</span><span> </span><span>Union wide </span><span>demand-side measures can help create lead markets for low-carbon and Union-produced energy-intensive industrial products, supporting decarbonisation while strengthening the Union’s industrial base.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(20)</span></span><span>Downstream sectors that account for a large share of demand for certain energy-intensive materials, such as the construction and automotive sectors, should be prioritised under this Regulation when establishing low-carbon requirements, Union origin requirements, or both. Th</span><span>at</span><span> is particularly appropriate given that </span><span>such</span><span> sectors are significantly subject to public procurement and support schemes, </span><span class="normaltextrun">wh</span><span class="normaltextrun">ile</span><span class="normaltextrun"> the </span><span>share</span><span class="normaltextrun"> of energy-intensive input in total production value is relatively small </span><span class="normaltextrun">and therefore</span><span class="normaltextrun"> </span><span class="normaltextrun">minimises</span><span class="normaltextrun"> the impact of any price premium</span><span class="normaltextrun">.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(21)</span></span><span>In order to ensure regulatory consistency with existing Union product legislation, steel, concrete and aluminium in construction should be considered low-carbon in </span><span>compliance </span><span>with the requirements set out in the implementing measures adopted pursuant to Regulation</span><span>s</span><span> (EU) 2024/3110</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref32" href="#footnote32">32</a>
               </span><span> </span><span>and (EU) 2024/1781</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref33" href="#footnote33">33</a>
               </span><span> </span><span>of the European Parliament and of the Council</span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(22)</span></span><span>The Clean Industrial Deal Communication</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref34" href="#footnote34">34</a>
               </span><span> </span><span>highlighted the need to create lead markets for industrial products with a low greenhouse gas emissions intensity, including by promoting such products on the internal market through</span><span> </span><span>the establishment of a Union labelling scheme, starting with the steel sector. Th</span><span>at</span><span> should be seen in the context of Union products legislation already designed to introduce labelling and information requirements, including comprehensive product labelling requirements to be established under the delegated acts pursuant to Regulation</span><span>s</span><span> (EU) 2024/3110 and (EU) 2024/1781.</span><span> </span><span>Considering the importance of both primary and secondary steel production for the long-term </span><span>resilience of the Union industrial base, such requirements should be based on classes of performance that acknowledge the different decarbonisation effort of the technologies</span><span>’</span><span> routes,</span><span> </span><span>also rewarding circularity, adjusting </span><span>emission intensity thresholds based on percentage of scrap metal used in production for those product categories that typically require primary steel production, as necessary.</span><span> </span><span>It should also be possible to complement the delegated acts adopted pursuant to Regulations (EU) 2024/3110 and (EU) 2024/1781 in order to support</span><span> </span><span>the creation of lead markets by informing investment decisions towards products granted a lower greenhouse gas intensity performance class, for industrial products not yet regulated by a Delegated Act under Regulation (EU) 2024/1781, or covered in the scope of products included in the working plan adopted in accordance with </span><span>that </span><span>Regulation. To do so, it should be possible to establish voluntary classification systems based on the greenhouse gas intensity of industrial products. To provide</span><span> environmental integrity</span><span> </span><span>and administrative feasib</span><span>ility</span><span>, it is </span><span>important to</span><span> rely on well-established and monitored emissions accounting methodologies. For domestic installations and sub-installations, the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) provides relevant products benchmarks and system boundaries in Annex I to Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/331</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref35" href="#footnote35">35</a>
               </span><span> and sound emissions accounting rules in Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/2066</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref36" href="#footnote36">36</a>
               </span><span>. Concerning imported products, in order to limit administrative burden, it is appropriate to enable the use of data already verified in the context of the Carbon Border Adjustments Mechanism (CBAM), in accordance with implementing rules adopted pursuant to Article 7(a) of Regulation (EU) 2023/956 of the European Parliament and of the Council</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref37" href="#footnote37">37</a>
               </span><span>. In view of reflecting accurately the greenhouse gas intensity of the industrial product, in addition to covering the direct emissions typically related to the installation’s activities covered by Annex I of Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref38" href="#footnote38">38</a>
               </span><span>, it is appropriate to also account for the most important sources of indirect emissions, including those from electricity, hydrogen and heat production used in the manufacturing process.</span><span> </span><span>To ensure consistency and limit administrative burden, methodologies </span><span>used to define low-carbon requirements under this Regulation </span><span>should make use of emissions </span><span>of data </span><span>reported under t</span><span>he</span><span> </span><span>EU ETS and CBAM</span><span>, where available and relevant</span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(23)</span></span><span>In order to </span><span>ensure </span><span>the attainment of </span><span>the objectives of this Regulation</span><span>, in particular</span><span> the creation of lead markets </span><span>for European </span><span>low-</span><span>carbon</span><span> </span><span>industrial</span><span> </span><span>prod</span><span>u</span><span>cts</span><span>, </span><span>minimum mandatory technical specifications should be provided for </span><span>l</span><span>ow</span><span>-carbon </span><span>and Union origin requirements in public procurement procedures </span><span>Those requirements should apply to the procurement of</span><span> </span><span>those products in public supply contracts </span><span>and </span><span>in public works, public services contracts and concessions, where those products will be used for activities conducted under those contracts. In compliance with the public procurement framework, those minimum mandatory technical specifications should avoid artificially restricting competition and avoid favouring a specific economic operator. Contracting authorities and contracting entities should conduct the public procurement procedures in compliance with Directives 2014/23/EU</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref39" href="#footnote39">39</a>
               </span><span>, 2014/24/EU</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref40" href="#footnote40">40</a>
               </span><span> and 2014/25/EU</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref41" href="#footnote41">41</a>
               </span><span> </span><span>of the European Parliament and of the Council </span><span>and applicable sectoral legislation. </span><span>The Union origin of products and components should be determined in accordance with the Union customs legislation. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(24)</span></span><span>In order to ensure the feasibility of the requirements at reasonable cost and avoid restricting competition, it is necessary to</span><span> lay down the conditions under which contracting authorities may, on an exceptional basis, decide not to apply the </span><span>low-carbon and Union origin</span><span> requirements. Those conditions should cover cases where the application of such requirements would result in technical incompatibilities in the operation or maintenance of a project</span><span> such as </span><span>situations where </span><span>the</span><span> use </span><span>of such products</span><span> would risk compromising the fulfilment of basic requirements for construction works </span><span>of the building or infrastructure, </span><span>set out in Regulation (EU) 2024/3110.</span><span> </span><span>The requirements laid down in this Regulation should apply exclusively to procurement procedures falling within</span><span> the </span><span>scope of Directive</span><span> 2014/23/EU, </span><span>Directive </span><span>2014/24/EU and </span><span>Directive </span><span>2014/25/EU, </span><span>that is,</span><span> to procedures whose estimated value reaches </span><span>or exceeds the </span><span>thresholds</span><span> </span><span>set out in those Directives. Accordingly,</span><span> procurement procedures </span><span>not covered by those Directives, including those below the applicable thresholds, should not be subject to the requirements established by this Regulation</span><span>, thereby avoiding disproportionate obligations for low-value procurements carried out by contracting authorities, including at local leve</span><span>l</span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(25)</span></span><span>The </span><span>Automotive package adopted on</span><span> 16 December 2025 </span><span>includes a proposal to</span><span> </span><span>amend Regulation (EU) 2019/631</span><span> </span><span>of the European Parliament and of the Council</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref42" href="#footnote42">42</a>
               </span><span> </span><span>to provide</span><span>, </span><span>inter alia</span><span>, for the granting of super-credits for small affordable electric vehicles made in the Union prior to 2035 and </span><span>amends</span><span> </span><span>the</span><span> 2035 emissions reduction target, with the remaining emissions to be compensated through the use of low-carbon steel made in the Union or renewable and low-carbon fuels. </span><span>The Automotive package also includes a </span><span>[</span><span>proposal </span><span>for a Regulation </span><span>on clean corporate vehicles</span><span>]</span><span> </span><span>which </span><span>limits</span><span> </span><span>financial support for</span><span> corporate vehicles to</span><span> zero- and low-emissions corporate vehicles</span><span> </span><span>‘</span><span>made in the European Union’</span><span>. </span><span>In order to ensure legal certainty and consistency with Regulation (EU) 2019/631</span><span> </span><span>as amended</span><span> and the </span><span>[</span><span>proposal for a Regulation on clean corporate vehicles</span><span>]</span><span>, this Regulation should lay down definitions of ‘small affordable electric vehicles made in the Union’</span><span>, </span><span>‘low-carbon steel made in the Union’</span><span> and ‘corporate cars</span><span> and vans made in the European Union’</span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(26)</span></span><span>In order to simplify procedures and reduce administrative burden, the verification of </span><span>compliance</span><span> with the requirements laid </span><span>down</span><span> in this Regulation should not impose a disproportionate burden on economic operators or contracting authorities. The verification system should therefore be based on a self-declaration by economic operators. </span><span>Such</span><span> approach is consistent with the general framework for public procurement established by Directive 2014/24/EU, in particular Article 59 thereof, which provides for self-declaration of compliance, subject to subsequent verification</span><span> of the successful tenderer</span><span>.</span><span> </span><span>For vehicles, </span><span>manufacturers should, at the time of issuing the certificate of conformity </span><span>in accordance with</span><span> Regulation (EU) 2018/858</span><span> </span><span>of the European Parliament and of the Council</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref43" href="#footnote43">43</a>
               </span><span>, provide an accompanying document certifying </span><span>for the vehicles that comply</span><span> with the relevant Union origin requirements. </span><span>This document should be equivalent to a self-declaration and form part of the documentary evidence demonstrating compliance with the requirements set out in this Regulation.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(27)</span></span><span>To ensure that the requirements established by this Regulation remain appropriate even as market conditions, technological developments and the climate and </span><span>internal</span><span> m</span><span>arket policy objectives </span><span>of the Union </span><span>continue to evolve, the Commission should be empowered to revise the requirements based on objective criteria and monitoring results. When assessing whether to revise Union origin requirements, low-carbon requirements, or both, the Commission should take into account developments in the relevant legislative frameworks, including the </span><span>customs legislation on rules of origin, </span><span>Emissions Trading System</span><span> laid down in </span><span>Directive 2003/87/EC</span><span> the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism</span><span> </span><span>laid down in </span><span>Regulation (EU) 2023/956</span><span>, and trade defence instruments.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(28)</span></span><span>Investment, including from foreign entities, plays a critical role in fostering a strong internal market</span><span> and territorial cohesion</span><span>, particularly by promoting innovation and driving economic growth in the Union which is essential for its competitiveness. However,</span><span> in exceptional circumstances, particularly large investments originating from third countries that hold a very significant market position in the global risk disrupting important supply chains and the security of emerging strategic sectors that are of particular importance in the development of the internal market.</span><span> </span><span>D</span><span>ivergent conditions applied by Member States </span><span>for such investments </span><span>fragment the internal market by creating unequal conditions for investors allowing investments that do not contribute genuine added value to the Union economy</span><span> while creating significant risk for the development and supply security in these sectors</span><span> and </span><span>creating </span><span>an incentive for “</span><span>regulatory arbitrage</span><span>” by investors. </span><span>Allowing such investments to proceed without any conditions</span><span> </span><span>could mean that</span><span> the added value creation associated with </span><span>selected</span><span> strategic technologies and innovative </span><span>manufacturing</span><span> activities remains outside the Union</span><span>, which have detrimental effect for the Union’s supply security and technological development in emerging strategic sectors</span><span>. </span><span>Moreover, unconditional exposure of the internal market to such large investments risks putting into question the Union’s technological advancements necessary for its twin transition and defence capabilities. Therefore, the provisions of this Regulation should ensure that such large investments coming from third countries that hold a particularly significant market position do not disrupt the Union’s supply security and economic security, and ensure its technological advancement in emerging strategic sectors. If such investments do not provide for sufficient Union participation and technology transfer, the long-term supply security of emerging strategic sectors is hampered due to lack of Union capacities independent from the country holding a significant share of relevant global supply. Furthermore, it has been observed that certain of such investments do not involve meaningful employment of Union workers, which jeopardizes the development of skills crucial for the development of emerging strategic sectors in the internal market.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(29)</span></span><span>In order to ensure that the internal market remains attractive for investment, and that investment adds value to the Union’s economy and society, it is necessary to</span><span> establish common c</span><span>onditions</span><span> for foreign direct investment in </span><span>manufacturing</span><span> emerging strategic sectors. </span><span>Those sectors</span><span> should be</span><span> manufacturing</span><span> sectors with innovative potential where Union entities are not at or near the global innovation frontier</span><span>, and where appropriate Union capacities and participation should be ensured. Harmonised</span><span> criteria</span><span> </span><span>should apply to foreign investors of a third country which holds over 40% of the global manufacturing capacity in emerging strategic sectors. </span><span>To ensure the effectiveness of the provisions of this Regulation, t</span><span>he Commission should monitor the global manufacturing capacity of th</span><span>o</span><span>se sectors and publish </span><span>the results</span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(30)</span></span><span>Greenfield foreign </span><span>investments occur where the foreign investor or a foreign investor’s subsidiary in the Union sets up new facilities or a new undertaking in the Union. Both Greenfield and Brownfield foreign investments should fall within the scope of this Regulation</span><span> to the extent that they involve the acquisition of control over a Union target or Union asset</span><span>, as they both have the possibility to impact the well-functioning internal market.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(31)</span></span><span>The review of the investments and application of the harmonised conditions should be carried out in accordance with this Regulation. It should take into account all information available and adhere to the principle of proportionality. Moreover, </span><span>all measures taken by national authorities or the Commission with respect to</span><span> the </span><span>review</span><span> of foreign investments should comply with Union law, and in particular with Articles 49 and 63 TFEU. </span>
            </p>
         </div>
         <div class="content">
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(32)</span></span><span>The</span><span>refore, the</span><span> provisions of this Regulation should apply to foreign direct investments in emerging strategic sectors </span><span>in accordance with</span><span> the thresholds established by this Regulation, notwithstanding the screening mechanism established under Regulation (EU) 2019/452</span><span> </span><span>of the European Parliament and of the Council</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref44" href="#footnote44">44</a>
               </span><span>. Moreover, the provisions of this Regulation should </span><span>also </span><span>apply without prejudice to Union competition law instruments, including Regulation (EU) 2022/2560 </span><span>of the European Parliament and of the Council</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref45" href="#footnote45">45</a>
               </span><span> </span><span>and Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref46" href="#footnote46">46</a>
               </span><span>. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(33)</span></span><span>The foreign direct investment criteria should capture emerging strategic sector investments in the Union by third-country investors (‘foreign investors’) in the Union. However, it could also be necessary to include investments in the Union by entities that are controlled, directly or indirectly, by a third-country person or entity regardless of the ultimate owner’s location (‘foreign investor’s subsidiary’), as they are equally capable of disrupting the functioning of the internal market, including its supply and economic security, due to the control exercised from the third country having a </span><span>significant</span><span> market share</span><span> </span><span>Therefore, Investment Authorities should apply the investment criteria where they are clearly needed to effectively ensure the protection of public security, the supply and economic security, and environmental sustainability in the Union, and where it is essential for the technological advancements of the internal market for the green and digital transition and defence purposes. Moreover, to prevent the circumvention of the Regulation’s provisions, where no alternative</span><span> measures are reasonably available</span><span>.</span><span> To ensure the proportional application of conditions prescribed to investments made by the foreign investor’s subsidiary, the Commission should have the opportunity to assess the notification and request the Investment Authority to prescribe certain conditions. Apart from review of foreign direct investments made by the foreign investor’s subsidiary as established by this Regulation, investments coming from other Union Member States should not be conditioned or deterred.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(34)</span></span><span>It is necessary to </span><span>ensure a lasting link between the foreign investor and the Union target, whether it is carried out directly by a foreign investor or through an entity established in the Union and controlled by a foreign investor. </span><span>However, </span><span>that</span><span> should not apply to the acquisition of company securities that are intended purely for financial investment and without any intention to influence the management or control of the company (‘portfolio investments’).</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(35)</span></span><span>Restructuring operations within a corporate group and investments made in financial institutions in application of a resolution tool as well as of write down and conversion powers should fall outside of the scope of this Regulation. Internal restructurings should only be excluded from the scope of application to the extent that they are conducted solely for the purpose of the internal reorganisation of a Union target or of the corporate group to which the Union target belongs, without resulting in any changes in the beneficial ownership </span><span>or control </span><span>of the Union target. In particular, internal restructurings should be excluded where they do not result in a situation where a new foreign investor acquires ownership or control over the Union target or over a company that directly or indirectly owns or controls that Union target, where there is an increase in the shares held by foreign investors, or where the transaction results in additional rights for foreign investors that may lead to a change in the effective participation of one or more foreign investors in the management or control of the Union target.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(36)</span></span><span>The </span><span>foreign direct investment criteria</span><span> should only apply to emerging strategic sector foreign direct investments reaching an investment value threshold that is able to disrupt the functioning of the internal market. A threshold of EUR 100 million should be considered as having potential for </span><span>to impact the well-functioning of </span><span>the internal market</span><span> </span><span>in emerging strategic sectors. Such foreign direct investment covered by the scope of this Regulation would bear high risk </span><span>on the security and environmental sustainability of the Union, while</span><span> not producing enough added value </span><span>including ensuring Union contribution in the investment, enhancement of the Union’s technological development, employment of Union workers and contribution to Union value chains</span><span> for the internal market</span><span> </span><span>without compliance with the </span><span>harmonised</span><span> conditions. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(37)</span></span><span>In order to ensure the effective application of this Regulation, each Member State should designate an investment authority responsible for assessing the conditions of investment by foreign entities in emerging strategic sectors. Moreover, it should be equipped with the legal, administrative, and financial resources to carry out its tasks effectively and independently, with due regard to the authorities already responsible for implementing </span><span>Regulation (EU) 2019/452</span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(38)</span></span><span>To enable Member States to effectively identify </span><span>the </span><span>investments</span><span> defined in this Regulation</span><span>, foreign investors should notify competent authorities prior to acquiring or establishing significant stakes in undertakings or assets within the Union. Setting a threshold at </span><span>3</span><span>0 percent </span><span>ownership or other rights establishing control</span><span> for both undertakings and assets should ensure that the mechanism captures investments capable of </span><span>impacting the well-functioning of </span><span>the internal market. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(39)</span></span><span>To minimise the risk of circumvention through fragmented or indirect acquisitions, where several foreign investors act in concert, or where investments are made through affiliated entities or complex ownership structures, their respective interests should be aggregated </span><span>by the Investment Authority </span><span>for the purpose of determining the investment value and the notification threshold. Aggregation should also apply to existing holdings in the same Union undertaking or asset, whether direct or indirect, individual or joint, to ensure that successive transactions leading to significant influence or control are duly notified. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(40)</span></span><span>In order</span><span> to</span><span> </span><span>ensure Union participation in large foreign direct investments originating from third countries having a significant global position, </span><span>this Regulation should establish limits on the extent of ownership and control that foreign investors </span><span>can</span><span> acquire in Union undertakings and assets. Accordingly, foreign investors should not, whether directly or indirectly, establish, acquire, hold, or exercise ownership interests exceeding 49% of the share capital, voting rights, or equivalent ownership interests in any Union target, nor establish or obtain equivalent ownership, leasehold, or other rights conferring control over a Union asset.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(41)</span></span><span>To ensure that foreign investors and Union entities cooperate in emerging strategic sectors while ensuring sufficient participation of Union partners, joint venture requirements should be prescribed</span><span>, which should include contractual arrangements</span><span>. </span><span>In the joint venture, the</span><span> foreign investor should not </span><span>hold more than 49 % </span><span>of the</span><span> share capital, voting rights, or equivalent ownership interests or other rights conferring control in any of the Union entities participating in the joint venture.</span><span> Th</span><span>at</span><span> condition should also contribute to the strategic autonomy of the Union and ensure value added to the internal market.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(42)</span></span><span>It is necessary to assess, as part of the conditions </span><span>for approval of</span><span> a foreign direct investment, whether the transfer of technology </span><span>can contribute to achieving </span><span>the objectives of this Regulation. </span><span>To that end</span><span>, the foreign investors </span><span>shou</span><span>ld</span><span> </span><span>be encouraged to</span><span> license to the Union Target, the joint venture or the legal entity acquiring or owning the Union asset the relevant intellectual property rights,</span><span> and </span><span>know-how, </span><span>which are </span><span>necessary for carrying out the concerned economic activity in the context of the foreign direct investment. Appropriate intellectual property licensing agreement(s) should therefore be </span><span>granted</span><span> by the foreign investor to the Union Target, the joint venture or the legal entity acquiring or owning the Union asset. The scope and conditions of these agreements, such as the exact IP rights concerned, the exclusive nature of the license, the duration of the license or confidentiality-preserving measures, should be appropriate to the circumstances and to the objective pursued under this Regulation and the relevant investment. The foreign investor should </span><span>commit to granting</span><span> the appropriate </span><span>licens</span><span>es</span><span> of intellectual property rights and </span><span>relevant</span><span> know-how</span><span> they hold, as required for the economic activity concerned</span><span>.</span><span> </span><span>That</span><span> could be achieved by providing a description of the main aspects of the </span><span>possible </span><span>licensing agreements, on a confidential basis, with the </span><span>Investment</span><span> Authority. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(43)</span></span><span>Where the Union Target or the legal entity acquiring or owning the Union asset </span><span>owns intellectual property rights in</span><span> </span><span>an invention, a work or any other asset subject to intellectual property protection</span><span> prior to the foreign investment</span><span>, </span><span>those</span><span> intellectual property rights should fully and exclusively </span><span>remain under the control of</span><span> the Union Target or the legal entity acquiring or owning the Union asset. The foreign investor should not claim any intellectual property right nor undertake any activity that would affect the ability of the Union Target or the legal entity acquiring or owning the Union asset to </span><span>own and exercise the</span><span> </span><span>intellectual property rights on </span><span>their</span><span> </span><span>inventions, works, trademarks, designs or any other relevant asset</span><span> obtained prior to the foreign investment</span><span>.</span><span> </span><span>Where</span><span> an invention, a work or any other asset subject to intellectual property protection is the result of a collaborative work between the Union Target or the legal entity acquiring or owning the Union asset and the foreign investor or as a result of the joint venture, the intellectual property rights should be owned jointly by the foreign investor, the Union Target or the legal entity acquiring or owning the Union asset, depending on the circumstances. The conditions accompanying the co-ownership of intellectual property rights should, to the extent possible, be defined and communicated to the </span><span>Investment</span><span> Authority, ahead of the approval of the foreign direct investment. These conditions should include clarifications as to the possibility for one co-owner to grant a licence and start infringement procedures as well as the financial agreements as regards the filing and registration of intellectual property rights and licensing agreements. In the case of a joint venture</span><span> without a legal personality</span><span>, clarifications should be provided to the </span><span>Investment</span><span> Authority </span><span>regarding the ownership </span><span>of intellectual property.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(44)</span></span><span>It is necessary to ensure </span><span>that the </span><span>foreign </span><span>investors’ expertise</span><span> of the large foreign direct investment under the scope of this Regulation</span><span> should </span><span>contribute to </span><span>enhancing </span><span>the Union’s </span><span>technological development both within and outside the Union Target, the joint venture or the </span><span>legal entity acquiring or owning the Union asset</span><span>. To that end, foreign investors should invest in research and development projects to be executed within the Union</span><span> while</span><span> ensuring that the Union will benefit from the results produced</span><span>. </span><span>It is therefore necessary to assess, as part of the conditions to be considered for having a foreign direct investment approved, whether the </span><span>foreign </span><span>investors’ research and development investments are </span><span>adequate to achieve that objective</span><span>. Such</span><span> investments </span><span>could be directed </span><span>to </span><span>the benefit of</span><span> research institutions</span><span> established in the Union</span><span>, including in</span><span> the context of</span><span> joint projects </span><span>with</span><span> the </span><span>Union</span><span> </span><span>T</span><span>arget</span><span>, the joint venture or the </span><span>legal entity acquiring or owning the Union asset</span><span>. Those</span><span> investments </span><span>could also</span><span> be made within the </span><span>Union</span><span> target</span><span>, the joint venture or the </span><span>legal entity acquiring or owning the Union asset</span><span>, for developing or executing specific research and development activities. These </span><span>investments could also consist in the</span><span> training </span><span>of Union</span><span> workers</span><span>, or</span><span> direct or indirect financial support to research and </span><span>development projects within the Union Target, the joint venture or the </span><span>legal entity acquiring or owning the Union asset</span><span>. Any assessment performed in relation to investments in research and development projects to be executed within the Union should be without prejudice to Union competition law instruments, including Regulations (EU) 2022/2560 and (EC) No 139/2004.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(45)</span></span><span>To promote sustainable integration of investments by foreign entities to the internal market</span><span> </span><span>and the development of skills in emerging strategic sectors, and to ensure meaningful social contribution at the place of the investment, such investments </span><span>should </span><span>employ a proportion of Union workers and </span><span>should provide</span><span> appropriate training and capacity-building measures, involving education and training providers, as well as social partners. The foreign investor should ensure that the thresholds established in this Regulation are fulfilled across all categories of workforce, including the operational, technical, supervisory, and managerial positions. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(46)</span></span><span>To strengthen the industrial capacity of emerging strategic sectors and to integrate foreign direct investment into the Union’s industrial ecosystem, </span><span>a certain share of </span><span>inputs manufactured in the Union </span><span>should be</span><span> included in products placed on the Union market by such investments. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(47)</span></span><span>In order to ensure that foreign direct investments fulfil </span><span>at least 4 of the 6 </span><span>conditions established by this Regulation, the </span><span>competent </span><span>Investment Authority should examine each notification and issue a reasoned decision on its approval or rejection. Investment Authorities should establish the fulfilment of the conditions, or as appropriate, the intent of the foreign investor to comply with the conditions. Such investments should not be implemented without the explicit approval of the Investment Authority. Accordingly, foreign investors should comply with a set of conditions before starting their economic activity</span><span> regarding the relevant foreign direct investment</span><span>. </span><span>Investment Authorities should decide </span><span>in a timeframe ensuring both procedural efficiency and legal certainty. Where justified by the complexity of the case or the need for additional information, </span><span>that timeframe</span><span> </span><span>could</span><span> be extended, for </span><span>justified and</span><span> duly substantiated</span><span> reasons</span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(48)</span></span><span>Member States should inform the Commission </span><span>about</span><span> notifications received to allow the Commission to effectively monitor the investment landscape and ensure a harmonised investment framework across the internal market. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(49)</span></span><span>In order to ensure the horizontal application of this Regulation </span><span>in</span><span> the internal market, the Commission should be </span><span>able</span><span> to provide an opinion on whether the investment fulfils the conditions set out in this Regulation. </span><span>Such</span><span> opinion </span><span>should</span><span> be made publicly available. If </span><span>the Investment Authority intends to diverge from the Commission opinion in its decision, it should</span><span> extend the approval process for two additional months in order to properly assess the Commission's arguments. When taking a decision, Member States should justify how they took the Commission’s opinion into account. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(50)</span></span><span>In order to ensure the horizontal application of this Regulation on the </span><span>Single Market</span><span>, the Commission should </span><span>be able</span><span> to review foreign direct investments, based on its own initiative </span><span>or on</span><span> the initiative of a Member State affected by the foreign direct investment. </span><span>That</span><span> should be particularly the case for investments where several member states are impacted, as well as high value investments and investments with particular strategic importance for the Union due to their effect on the </span><span>Single Market</span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(51)</span></span><span>The Investment Authorities should not only ensure compliance with the conditions at the time of </span><span>the foreign direct investment’s</span><span> notification, but also throughout its operation, as appropriate, to </span><span>ensure</span><span> that the benefits of the foreign direct investment are maximised on the internal market.</span>
            </p>
         </div>
         <div class="content">
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(52)</span></span><span>To ensure that </span><span>foreign direct</span><span> investment criteria for the emerging strategic sectors remain appropriate even as market conditions, technological developments and the competitiveness policy objectives </span><span>of the Union </span><span>continue to evolve, the Commission should </span><span>monitor </span><span>the global manufacturing trends of </span><span>strategic sectors and</span><span> </span><span>be empowered to adopt implementing acts imposing foreign investment criteria to additional strategic sectors</span><span>.</span><span> </span><span>The</span><span> Commission should assess in particular the threshold value, as well as whether all of the investment criteria referred to in this regulation are appropriate and necessary to meet the objectives of this regulation. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(53)</span></span><span>Clustering industrial activity</span><span> </span><span>can contribute substantially to achieving the objectives of this Regulation and to strengthening </span><span>certain </span><span>strategic sectors in the internal market. </span><span>It is therefore appropriate to </span><span>promote the development of </span><span>industrial manufacturing acceleration areas</span><span>. Such areas should be limited in geographical scope in order to foster industrial symbiosis. When designating the areas, Member States should, in cooperation with regional authorities where appropriate, take into account industrial production </span><span>(in particular for certain strategic sectors) and their regions’ general level of</span><span> development, </span><span>with a focus on the less developed regions and those in transition</span><span>. </span><span>Furthermore, in order to strengthen the resilience, strategic autonomy and competitiveness of the Union’s industrial base, the designation of </span><span>industrial manufacturing acceleration areas</span><span> should align with strategic projects and other Union initiatives such as Net-Zero Acceleration Valleys</span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(54)</span></span><span>The industrial acceleration measures </span><span>within</span><span> the acceleration areas should seek appropriate synergies with other Union initiatives, including strategic projects recognised in Union legislation</span><span>, Net-Zero Acceleration Valleys and Union funding opportunities,</span><span> </span><span>in order</span><span> to align the strategic priorities in the internal market</span><span> </span><span>and benefit industrial installations vital for the strategic autonomy and competitiveness</span><span> of the Union</span><span>. Th</span><span>o</span><span>se benefits should also apply to undertakings awarded with the competitiveness seal under Regulation (EU) XXXX/[XX]</span><span class="FootnoteReference"> </span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref47" href="#footnote47">47</a>
               </span><span> (European Competitiveness Fund), unless specifically excluded by the Member State</span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(55)</span></span><span>To enable an adequate supply of critical raw materials for projects in the acceleration areas, the European Critical Raw Materials Board </span><span>established</span><span> by Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 should provide a platform to exchange information on critical raw materials related supply chain bottlenecks in the acceleration areas. </span><span>It should be possible for p</span><span>rojects in relevant areas </span><span>to</span><span> benefit from the Joint purchasing mechanism established in Article 25 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 to aggregate their demand for strategic raw materials and increase their negotiating power with potential sellers, especially when they contain </span><span>small or medium-sized enterprises (</span><span>SMEs</span><span>)</span><span> and </span><span>small mid-cap companies (</span><span>SMCs</span><span>)</span><span>. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(56)</span></span><span>Sufficient and timely energy supply to the acceleration areas constitutes a fundamental enabling condition for their effective deployment and for the development of manufacturing activities. Reliable and accurate information on future energy demand contribute</span><span>s</span><span> to cost-effective grid development. Member States should therefore prepare an analysis for each acceleration area, identifying its future energy needs. </span><span>Such</span><span> analysis should serve the purpose of providing information for the national grid planning thereby contributing to purposeful anticipatory grid investments and faster energy connections for the acceleration area. When defining the scope, Member States should take into account the availability of relevant transport and network infrastructure</span><span>. </span><span>The results of these assessments </span><span>should be reflected in national network development plans to adequately capture future points of energy demand in upcoming grid planning. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(57)</span></span><span>Where</span><span> </span><span>industrial manufacturing</span><span> acceleration areas</span><span> are set up</span><span>, their designation should correspond to the potential to access or organise education and training opportunities to ensure the availability of skilled labour. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(58)</span></span><span>To promote the development of </span><span>industrial manufacturing acceleration areas</span><span> and to expedite the permit-granting procedures necessary for industrial activities within those areas, Member States should establish an aggregated baseline permit reflecting the specific characteristics of each identified industrial acceleration area and tailored to the industrial manufacturing sector or sectors to be deployed therein. That aggregated baseline permit </span><span>issued by public authorities</span><span> should cover the permits commonly required for such activities within the area, excluding those permits that are installation specific, such as those required under Directive</span><span> 2010/75/EU of </span><span>the </span><span>European Parliament</span><span> and </span><span>of the Council</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref48" href="#footnote48">48</a>
               </span><span> and the grid connection permit</span><span>. Consequently, project promoters should be required to obtain additional permits only for activities not covered by the aggregated baseline permit as well as environmental assessments where required. </span><span>In case of activities potentially affecting Union and nationally protected sites, relevant permits should be granted only after having ensured that the activities are compatible with the conservation objectives of these sites. </span><span>Such approach should significantly accelerate permit-granting procedures and reduce the administrative burden associated with them</span><span> </span><span>whilst maintaining high level of environmental standards</span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(59)</span></span><span>In order to establish a framework to ensure the </span><span>Union’s strategic autonomy and economic security through access to a secure, sustainable and resilient supply of relevant manufacturing products, the power to adopt acts in accordance with Article 290 </span><span>TFEU should be delegated to the Commission in respect of changes to the list of </span><span>third countries</span><span> whose content </span><span>is not</span><span> </span><span>treated as equivalent to Union origin</span><span>,</span><span> the introduction or amendment of Union origin and low-carbon requirements, including for additional net-zero technologies and for products and services listed in Annexes II and III</span><span>,</span><span> </span><span>laying</span><span> down Union-level demand-side measures for products from the chemical industry</span><span>, taking into account, among others, recommendations from the Critical Chemicals Alliance, </span><span>the extension of foreign direct investment criteria to additional emerging strategic sectors</span><span>,</span><span> the specification of common procedural rules for foreign direct investment criteria</span><span>, and</span><span> establishing </span><span>classification systems based on</span><span> the greenhouse gas intensity </span><span>for </span><span>products</span><span>.</span><span> </span><span>It is of particular importance that the Commission carries out appropriate consultations during its preparatory work, including at expert level, and that those consultations be conducted in accordance with the principles laid down in the Inter-institutional</span><span> Agreement of 13 April 2016</span><span> </span><span>on Better Law-Making</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref49" href="#footnote49">49</a>
               </span><span>. In particular, to ensure equal participation in the preparation of delegated acts, the European Parliament and the Council receive all documents at the same time as Member States’ experts, and their experts systematically have access to meetings of Commission expert groups dealing with the preparation of delegated acts.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(60)</span></span><span>In order to ensure uniform conditions for the implementation of this Regulation, implementing powers should be conferred on the Commission as regards specifying</span><span> </span><span>the method for calculating the proportion of </span><span>volume of products and components</span><span> originating in the Union</span><span> and </span><span>for verifying the </span><span>compliance with the conditions laid down in Article 15</span><span>.</span><span> Those powers should be exercised in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 182/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref50" href="#footnote50">50</a>
               </span><span>.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(61)</span></span><span>The Commission should evaluate this Regulation based on the information provided by Member States. Pursuant to paragraph 22 of the Interinstitutional Agreement on Better Law-Making of 13 April 2016, </span><span>such</span><span> evaluation should be based on the five criteria of efficiency, effectiveness, relevance, coherence and Union value added. It should also serve as the basis for impact assessments of possible further </span><span>measures.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(62)</span></span><span>To ensure compliance with the obligations laid down in this Regulation, Member States should provide for penalties to be imposed on undertakings that do not comply with their obligations. </span><span>Such</span><span> penalties should be without prejudice and in addition to specific penalty requirements set out by this Regulation, for instance on </span><span>foreign </span><span>direct investments. It is therefore necessary that Member States lay down effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties in national law for failure to comply with this Regulation. It is also necessary for Member States to ensure that project promoters have access, where relevant, to administrative or judicial review in accordance with national law.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(63)</span></span><span>When reviewing this Regulation, the Commission should assess the need to amend the provisions </span><span>included</span><span> in Chapters III and IV. In particular, it should consider </span><span>introducing</span><span> targeted Union origin in transport sectors critical to the Union’s economic security, notably building of ships and building of rail rolling stock. The Commission should also consider </span><span>introducing</span><span> an enhanced review of foreign direct investments for aeronautical products and parts.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(64)</span></span><span>Regulation (EU) 2018/1724 of the European Parliament and of the Council</span><span class="FootnoteReference">
                  <a class="footnoteRef" id="footnoteref51" href="#footnote51">51</a>
               </span><span>, which established the Single Digital Gateway, provides general rules for the online provision of information, procedures and assistance services that are relevant to the functioning of the </span><span>internal market</span><span>. In order to allow businesses and manufacturing industry project promoters, including for cross-border projects, to directly enjoy the benefits of the </span><span>internal market</span><span> </span><span>without incurring an unnecessary additional administrative burden</span><span>, t</span><span>he information that needs to be submitted to any relevant authorities as part of the permit-granting process under this Regulation is </span><span>that set out</span><span> in Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2018/1724. The related procedures are included in Annex II to that Regulation to ensure that project promoters can benefit from fully online procedures and the Once-Only Technical System Services. In particular, promoters of manufacturing industry projects should be able to fully access and complete any procedure related to the permit-granting process online, in accordance with Article 6(1) of </span><span>Regulation (EU) 2018/1724</span><span> </span><span>and Annex II </span><span>of that </span><span>Regulation.</span><span> </span><span>Regulation</span><span> (EU) 2018/1724 should therefore be amended accordingly.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(65)</span></span><span>Regulation (EU) 2024/1735 introduces resilience requirements for a range of net-zero technology final products. </span><span>Those requirements</span><span> </span><span>aim at</span><span> reduc</span><span>ing</span><span> dependencies on individual third countries of supply, but they are not sufficient to enable Union industries to scale up the potential of the internal market and carry a risk of circumvention. </span><span>Therefore</span><span>,</span><span> in order to address such challenges</span><span>, the legislative framework should ensure the need to attract and retain technological know-how within the Union</span><span>, through</span><span> targeted additional intervention. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(66)</span></span><span>The provisions on public procurement laid down in this Regulation should build on the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2024/1735 on resilience; and complement them by introducing additional requirements for battery energy storage systems, solar photovoltaic technologies, heat pumps, onshore and offshore wind technologies, </span><span>electrolysers</span><span> </span><span>and nuclear fission energy technologies. Such additional requirements should ensure that a certain share of the products and their main specific components originate in the Union. Th</span><span>at</span><span> approach should ensure sufficient diversification while strengthening strategic manufacturing capacity and technological sovereignty within the Union.</span><span> </span><span>The system for verification of compliance </span><span>with the requirements</span><span> should </span><span>limit the</span><span> administrative burden</span><span> and align with common public procurement practice </span><span>as well as</span><span> the </span><span>existing system of </span><span>verification of compliance under Regulation</span><span> </span><span>(EU) 2024/1735. It should therefore</span><span> rely on a self-declaration by economic operators.</span><span> </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(67)</span></span><span>In addition to complementing the public procurement provisions of Regulation (EU) 2024/1735, this Regulation should also </span><span>amend</span><span> them</span><span> to provide greater legal certainty</span><span>. The scope of Article 25 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1735 should be limited to those net-zero technologies for which public procurement of a relevant scale is expected to take place, thereby enhancing the clarity of the provision. </span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(68)</span></span><span>In line with the same policy objective pursued for renewable energy auctions under Regulation (EU) 2024/1735, this Regulation should extend the additional Union origin requirements to renewable energy auctions</span><span> for certain renewable energy technologies</span><span>,</span><span> in order to</span><span> contribute to strengthening the Union’s industrial base and ensuring resilience of net-zero technology supply chains. To reflect the specific characteristics of renewable energy auctions, the </span><span>additional </span><span>requirements should apply to the net-zero technologies that are most relevant in the context of auctions, which are battery energy storage systems, solar photovoltaic technologies, </span><span>electrolysers</span><span>, as well as on- and offshore wind technologies. Where Union origin requirements apply to auctions, other provisions setting similar requirements for public support schemes should not apply to those auctions.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(69)</span></span><span>To reinforce the effectiveness of the framework, and to reflect recent increases in geopolitical risks and global market distortions, the share of auctions covered by the requirements should be increased and a higher cost threshold for the opt-out from </span><span>those</span><span> requirements should be </span><span>established</span><span>. </span><span>That</span><span> should also prevent excessive use of exemptions and provide an effective incentive to boost </span><span>Union</span><span> production of renewable energy technologies.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(70)</span></span><span>Businesses and households are an essential part of the demand for net-zero technologies</span><span> in the Union</span><span>. Public support schemes designed to support consumer demand for such products are important tools for strengthening the Union’s economic security and accelerating the green transition. </span><span>In order to </span><span>build on the provisions </span><span>of Regulation (EU) 2024/1735</span><span> on resilience</span><span>, it is necessary to</span><span> complement </span><span>those provisions </span><span>introducing additional requirements for battery energy storage systems, solar photovoltaic technologies</span><span> and</span><span> heat pumps. Such additional requirements should ensure that certain main specific components</span><span> and,</span><span> in </span><span>some cases, </span><span>the </span><span>whole final product</span><span>, originate in the Union. Th</span><span>at</span><span> approach is in line with the general objective of support schemes to promote socially-desirable outcomes</span><span>, in view of making progress on the ambitions of the European Pillar of Social Rights as well as environmental and climate objectives. Furthermore, it</span><span> should ensure sufficient diversification while strengthening strategic manufacturing capacity and technological sovereignty within the Union.</span><span> Public authorities in charge of support schemes should have the possibility either to condition the eligibility of the scheme to the fulfilment of the requirements, or to grant additional financial compensation when the requirements are fulfilled. In the latter case, the additional financial compensation should have an incentivising effect. However, if State aid is involved, the additional financial compensation should not exceed the applicable maximum aid intensity.</span>
            </p>
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
               <span class="num"><span>(71)</span></span><span>Digital technologies continue to transform the way we generate, distribute, and consume energy. </span><span>Such</span><span> digital evolution, while presenting unprecedented opportunities, has also introduced complexity and interdependence within modern energy systems, which are now susceptible to a growing array of cyber threats. The integration of digital technologies into energy systems increases the attack surface for malicious actors, who can exploit vulnerabilities to disrupt operations, steal sensitive data, or manipulate energy markets. Such disruptions not only threaten the security and stability of our energy infrastructure and continuous supply of energy but also have cascading effects on all sectors of the economy that rely on stable energy inputs. Furthermore, energy system disruptions could undermine investor confidence and deter investment in essential modernisation and decarbonisation efforts. Therefore, safeguarding the cybersecurity of these systems is paramount to ensuring economic security, maintaining trust, and fostering resilience against future challenges.</span>
            </p>
         </div>
         <div class="content">
            <p class="li ManualConsidrant">
